/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.headline: King Charles addresses summit as demands for slavery apology grow
/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.excerpt: King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain. “We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. “We can, however, learn from the past. “The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth,” he said. “That shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.” Charles said the more he had furthered his understanding “through listening, learning and looking”, the more committed he had become to building modern partnerships capable of addressing past wrongs. But the king stopped short of an apology or explicit support for reparations, instead pointing to education, employment, intra-Commonwealth trade and climate resilience as ways of tackling continuing hardship and disadvantage. “For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us, but we can choose how we set our sail,” he said.
/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.trail: Speaking in Antigua, the king did not give explicit support for reparations but said he wanted to ‘address past wrongs’

/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.headline: As King Charles visits the Caribbean, is the reparations movement approaching a tipping point?
/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.excerpt: The sun is starting to set in the Bahamas and the loud wash of the tide, which is always audible on Nassau’s Western Esplanade, is beginning to be drowned out by the sound of excited screams. King Charles is visiting the Caribbean archipelago, for which he is still the head of state, for the first time in more than 50 years and a youth rally attended by schoolchildren makes for a particularly welcoming crowd. Some have described the king’s nine-day tour of the Bahamas, Antigua and Guyana amid growing calls for reparations as a significant risk that may accelerate his removal as head of state from the six remaining Caribbean Commonwealth countries in which he still serves. King Charles was in the Bahamas before travelling to Antigua for the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting (Chogm), which is usually a collegial gathering of leaders, but has only just managed to keep enslavement and reparations off the formal agenda. As the summit gets under way today, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will begin talks about a formal apology with countries affected by Britain’s role in transatlantic enslavement. Those talks will include plans for a “debt reset” for Commonwealth countries facing higher costs on their debts. Writing last week in the Guardian, Burnham indicated he is open to the possibility of a formal apology, going further than any UK prime minister has before.

/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.headline: PM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apology
/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.excerpt: Andy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message. The prime minister was en route to the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No 10 said he would use the event to launch a “structured dialogue” into what form an apology might take. UK officials already at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the move, and that it could help talks on separate issues such as trade and the climate. In comments released by No 10 before Burnham’s arrival, the prime minister said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth. Downing Street has ruled out the idea of paying reparations after an apology, but Burnham is expected to set out plans at the summit for a system of debt restructuring for countries facing higher debt costs. “In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful force for good, bringing together a third of the global population, and I believe it is key that the UK plays its full role in that,” Burnham said.
/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.trail: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda

/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.headline: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
/world/2026/nov/04/debt-relief-aid-no-re.excerpt: As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said. But a likely interest rate hike, triggered by higher-than-expected inflation, while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder. Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday. He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting. The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation, according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University. “It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said. “He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot. “There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.” Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.

/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.headline: Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.excerpt: Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families. The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies. Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned. Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations. Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980. Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested. The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.trail: Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served

/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.headline: Australia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong Kong
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.excerpt: The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said. Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend. The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong. The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed. “We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday. “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts. “Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.” Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.trail: Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed

/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.headline: ‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El Niño
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.excerpt: Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region. Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027. The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”. Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño: ‘Climate risk maps’ in China In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees. Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat. In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.trail: From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date

/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.headline: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.excerpt: A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city. The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring. Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.” Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.” Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union. She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.trail: Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge

/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.headline: Unidentified Murder review – playful sendup of alien abduction and true crime influencers in Hong Kong
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.excerpt: Modestly scaled and intricately structured, Kwok Ka-Hei and Jack Lee Chun-Kit’s comedy is a capriciously playful send-up of true crime aficionados and wannabe influencers, done with affection rather than malice. It revolves around a (fictional) 25-year-old case that captivates the whole of Hong Kong. Back when they were seven, childhood friends Mark (Ling Man-lung) and Kit (Ronald Lam Tsz-kit) claimed to have witnessed the abduction by aliens of their classmate Ho in the woods of Tung Tau Hill. On the 25th anniversary of this supposed incident, the pair re-enter the internet’s consciousness after an interview on an online chatshow about unsolved mysteries. Cashing in on their viral fame, Mark’s girlfriend Man (Renci Yeung) hires actor Kim (Peter Chan Charm-man) to pretend to be Ho, all in the hope of racking up views on her social channels. Just when the cameras are all set up, Man watches in horror as the staged reunion leads to a real murder … or does it? The film unfolds in a series of increasingly tricksy complications and reversals. All of a sudden, apparent victims are revealed to be scheming masterminds, and vice versa. As most of the actions take place in the forest where the abduction supposedly occurred, the plot derives comic relief from the increasingly blurred line between truth and playacting.
/world/2026/nov/05/hong-kong-joshua-wong.trail: Childhood friends claim to have witnessed the disappearance of a schoolkid in this low-budget comedy caper that pushes limits of storytelling

/society/2026/nov/04/cocaine-overtakes-h.headline: New powerful synthetic opioids behind sharp rise in Scottish drug deaths
/society/2026/nov/04/cocaine-overtakes-h.excerpt: New forms of a powerful synthetic opioid have contributed to a sharp rise in Scottish drug deaths, with the latest data showing an 11% increase in fatalities last year Annual figures released by National Records of Scotland (NRS) on Wednesday recorded 1,133 drug-related deaths in 2025, 116 more than the previous year. The 2025 figures are the sixth highest on record. Opiates and opioids, which include drugs such as heroin, remain the most deadly drug types, implicated in 78% of all deaths. But the presence of nitazenes – a highly potent type of synthetic opioid – rose by more than 200%, from 76 deaths in 2024 to 247 in 2025. Maree Todd, the minister for mental wellbeing, public health, sport, alcohol and drugs, said an “increasingly toxic and unpredictable drugs supply” required “more coordinated action across the country”. Last year’s data showed Scotland’s lowest drug deaths since 2017, but the charity Scottish Drugs Forum (SDF) warned at the time that this was most likely a blip, masking a recent surge in synthetic opioids in Scotland’s illicit drug market. Unlike plant-derived drugs such as heroin, nitazenes are created in illegal laboratories and can be hundreds of times stronger than traditional opiates and opioids. They are also often mixed with other drugs, increasing the risks to users who do not always know what is present in the supply.
/society/2026/nov/04/cocaine-overtakes-h.trail: Eleven per cent increase in fatalities last year partly down to presence of nitazenes in Scotland’s illicit drug market

/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.headline: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.excerpt: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country. The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added. The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history. The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that, if it did, it would make that information public. The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.trail: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.headline: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.excerpt: Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May. This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment. A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters. The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August. Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.

/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.headline: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.excerpt: A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said. Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported. The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”. Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders. The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services.

/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.headline: ‘Behind every case, a person’: the man leading DRC’s Ebola fight on the human cost hidden behind the numbers
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.excerpt: The statistics, says the man responsible for overseeing the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), are meaningless. That it is now the largest outbreak, the most deadly strain, that 100 days have passed, that the death rates keep climbing, says Prof Pierre Akilimali, should never detract from the human tragedies at the centre of this virus. “It is behind those numbers that matters; it is the father, the child, the loved relative. Behind every case is a person and behind every person is a family. For us Congolese, we hold on to that as we work.” But Akilimali, of the DRC’s National Public Health Institute, and now the incident manager of the country’s multi-agency response, is certain that those numbers will keep on sharply rising. As of 24 August, the Bundibugyo variant of the virus had 5,656 confirmed cases and 2,715 deaths. “Let’s say in two months we will reach the peak and start seeing a decrease, but this is guesswork,” he says. “The honest thing is that we do not yet know. “What I can say is that as we are improving community engagement we expect to have more confirmed cases, so we need to be sure that treatment centres are able to cope with those increased numbers.” Akilimali, like most Congolese health workers involved in the Ebola response since the outbreak was first officially declared in May, has been working flat out.
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.trail: Prof Pierre Akilimali, who heads DR Congo’s response to an outbreak that has so far killed more than 2,700 people, says tackling the disease requires trust and respect

/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.headline: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.excerpt: Every day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends. “More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.” Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.” That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid. “I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses. Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said.
/world/2026/nov/04/british-healthcare-wo.trail: People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face

On 6 January, officers arrested a man at an address in Wandsworth, London. The charges comprise 12 allegations of rape; eight of actual bodily harm; two of assault by penetration; two of sexual assault; two of controlling and coercive behaviour; two of making an indecent image of a child; one of distribution of an indecent image of a child; one of stalking; one of making threats to kill; one of false imprisonment; one of criminal damage; one of theft; and one of causing or inciting the sexual exploitation of a child. Madgwick is scheduled to appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 25 November. A CPS spokesperson said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute George Madgwick for serious sexual offences, including multiple counts of rape. He has also been charged with making a threat to kill, false imprisonment and stalking.

/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.headline: Rent rises of up to 88% still passing in England despite Renters’ Rights Act
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.excerpt: The rent tribunal system is “not working for anyone”, tenants and landlords have said, as rent increases of up to 88% continue to be approved despite Labour’s pledge to curb unfair rises. Tenants are challenging rent increases in record numbers since the Renters’ Rights Act came into effect in May, making the process easier and less risky for renters. But tenants and landlords have said people are facing increasingly long delays for hearings, and that there is a lack of consistency in how “fair market rent” is being decided. Analysis of data from May to October by London Renters Union (LRU) showed 80% of tenants who went through the tribunal process saw their rent go up, by an average of £1,200 a year, although in most cases it was less than the landlord’s proposed increase. In 36% of cases, the landlord’s proposed increase was approved in full, and in 42% of cases the rent increase was reduced. In 16% of cases the rent increase was cancelled, and in 6% rent was lowered. In one case, a rent tribunal approved an 88% rent increase on a property in Dagenham. The tenant, who paid rent via housing benefit, argued the increase would lead to undue hardship but his monthly rent still went up from £1,200 to £2,250. In another case, a tenant who challenged a £17-a-month rent increase received a £200 rent decrease after the tribunal ruled the rent was actually too high. Tenants’ unions have expressed concern over rent increases of 30% or more being regularly approved.
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.trail: Exclusive: While tenants are challenging increases in record numbers, renters and landlords say system is ‘not working for anyone’

/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.headline: ‘This is direct’: positive early feedback from pilot community mental health hub in Cumbria
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.excerpt: The night Tamara first walked through the doors of Hope Haven, a new community mental health hub in the heart of Whitehaven, she was afraid. “Terrified, actually,” she says. “Like, my life was falling apart. I didn’t know how to stop it from hurting.” The 22-year-old, who works in children’s transport, had been in and out of therapy and counselling since she was 14, after being abused by an acquaintance as a child. After a lengthy legal process her abuser was sentenced, but the “mental challenge” of dealing with what had happened to her was not over. “I was having a really hard time at home, and my best friend told me that I could go and stay with her for a bit, but I needed to ask for help first, so she dropped me off here at like 11 o’clock at night,” she says. That night was a turning point: Tamara was seen immediately by a member of staff and offered an appointment for the next day. She believes that if she hadn’t been offered help at Hope Haven, she would still be at “rock bottom”. Hope Haven is part of a pilot scheme of six hubs across England. It offers preventive, open-access care 24/7, meaning people do not need a diagnosis or referral to access its services. Its alternative approach reflects concerns that more traditional NHS services have struggled to improve local wellbeing. In its first five months from March to July, about 3,000 people accessed support either digitally or in person.
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.trail: Hope Haven in Whitehaven is one of six trial open-access, 24/7 schemes in England offering preventive care

/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.headline: Newcastle hospital told woman whose unborn baby had died to go home and ‘book a slot to give birth’
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.excerpt: A woman whose unborn baby had died was sent home from hospital with a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth. Danielle Brown, 31, was seven months pregnant when she was first discharged from hospital with pre-eclampsia, a potentially life-threatening pregnancy complication. She returned to hospital days later, when scans revealed that her daughter, Maisie, had died. Brown said she was devastated to have to return home knowing the baby she was carrying was no longer alive. “When it was confirmed Maisie had died, we burst into tears. Nobody explained what had happened to Maisie,” she said. Brown, from North Shields in north-east England, said she was then “given a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth”. She said: “Hearing that with no compassion angered me so much.” Brown and her partner, Anthony Miller, were delighted to be expecting a baby but seven months into the pregnancy, in February 2023, she fell ill and was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia. Monitoring by doctors at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI), Newcastle, had also raised concerns about Maisie’s heart rate. A consultant obstetrician said Brown should remain in hospital until she gave birth, given her potentially life-threatening condition. However, she was discharged 24 hours later on 14 February after a review by a different consultant. A day later, Brown phoned the RVI’s maternity assessment unit with more concerns but was told she probably had a stomach bug.

/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.headline: Driver who dragged cyclist under his car jailed for life for murder
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.excerpt: A driver who ploughed into a headteacher who was cycling home from school and dragged him, trapped under his car, for more than a mile has been jailed for life. Simon Richardson, who ignored give-way signs at a junction before the collision, was told he must serve a minimum of 25 years after a jury last week found him guilty of murder. His victim, Michael Mullins, 56, was remembered by his family as their “anchor”. His wife said her life had been “brutally and callously torn apart”. Jailing Richardson, 35, on Monday, Mrs Justice Brunner KC said the defendant had shown an “astonishing degree of disregard for human life”. She said: “For every moment you carried on, you were knowingly using your heavy vehicle to cause serious injury to a man who was trapped, injured and completely helpless as a result of your actions. “You did that because you decided escaping from the scene of an accident was more important than a human life.” Mullins was cycling home from Stretford grammar school on the evening of 20 April when the 4x4 Richardson was driving crashed into him. He hit the bonnet and windscreen of Richardson’s Volvo XC90 and then went under it, becoming entangled in the suspension. Richardson continued to drive for more than a mile, knowing that the trapped cyclist was just inches under his feet, a trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court heard.
/uk-news/2026/nov/04/husband-who-invited.trail: Simon Richardson hit Michael Mullins, dragged him for more than a mile under his Volvo XC90, and ran him over

/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.headline: Labour’s pledge to level-up minimum wage for under-20s before next election in doubt
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.excerpt: Labour looks less likely to meet its manifesto pledge to equalise the minimum wage for younger workers before the next election, after the chancellor failed to guarantee the rise would happen within that timeframe. John Healey said on Sunday his party was “prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government”, including possible spending cuts. His comments came as a former adviser to Andy Burnham, the economist Andy Haldane, warned that UK public finances were in a perilous state and the government was “on a precipice” of a Liz Truss-style meltdown. Government sources expressed anger at the comments, saying the markets had responded positively to the budget. Healey said in interviews on Sunday that he wanted to take the minimum wage increase at a slower pace for younger workers. He said the government was still committed to the increase but failed to spell out when it would be achieved. In the budget, a rise in the minimum wage to £13.21 per hour was handed to adults, alongside a rise to £11.27 for under-21s. A larger rise for younger workers would have been needed to move towards equalisation. Speaking on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Healey said he would take equalising the rates “one step at a time”, amid fears a rise could exacerbate youth unemployment. Labour’s 2024 manifesto committed to closing the gap on pay for 18- to 20-year-olds, but last week’s budget brought in a blanket increase of 3.9%.
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.trail: Chancellor John Healey fails to guarantee equalisation with adult wage will happen in timeframe set out in manifesto

/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.headline: Higher training costs for older workers risks plan to tackle youth jobs crisis, employers say
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.excerpt: Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis. The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead. Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed. The chancellor, John Healey, is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country. However, business leaders urged the government to reconsider the plan to make training older workers more expensive. “It will just mean opportunities are shifted around instead of creating new ones,” said Robert Halfon, a former Conservative skills minister who is now the executive director of policy at the manufacturing lobby group Make UK. “We agree that getting young people back into employment and training is a moral and economic imperative. But making it more expensive for employers to train older workers isn’t the answer,” he added.
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.trail: Exclusive: Ministers planning overhaul of apprenticeship funding to increase cost of over-25s training, Guardian understands

/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.headline: Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.excerpt: Employers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis. The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead. Aiming to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work. With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled that boosting access to apprenticeships would be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people. The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time. After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships. Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people.

/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.headline: Neet rates higher in England’s smaller cities and towns than in biggest cities
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.excerpt: Smaller cities and towns across England have higher rates of young people not in employment, education or training than the nine largest cities, analysis shows. The Centre for Cities, an independent thinktank dedicated to improving the economies of the UK, used 2021 census data to work out the rates across 41 cities and towns in England. Of those places, 10 of the smallest cities and towns had higher rates of 16- to 24-year-olds out of employment and education – an average of 15.7% of their youth population, compared with an average of 13.9% across the nine largest cities. It comes amid a national debate over chronic youth unemployment in the UK, with the latest ONS data showing just under 1 million young people are not in employment, training or education (Neet). An interim report published by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn in May found that the UK was “at risk of a lost generation”, with young adults facing a “perfect storm” of challenges. His final report is expected soon after the budget on 28 October. The Centre for Cities analysis shows London (117,095) and Birmingham (44,995) have the highest number of Neets in absolute terms, representing rates of 13.1% and 15.9% respectively. The average Neet rate across England is 12.6%. In Blackpool, 2,660 of young people are not in education, employment or training, a rate of 21.2%. In Slough, 2,170 young people are Neet (14.1%). The Shropshire town of Telford has 2,780 Neets (15.1%).
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.trail: Initiatives to address youth employment crisis and offer training are being launched in towns such as Telford

/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.headline: Tories call for 5-year freeze on minimum wage to tackle youth unemployment
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.excerpt: A Conservative shadow minister has called for the government to freeze the minimum wage for five years, a move that could cost low-paid workers almost £9,000. The call came in a report from the Prosperity Institute thinktank, which carries an endorsement from Andrew Sharpe, the shadow business minister. Sharpe said in his endorsement that it was time to take action to address the low rate of young people in work. “With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training this report is timely and its recommendations very sound. The government should adopt them in full,” the Conservative peer said. The paper recommends freezing the “national living wage” at £12.71 for five years and abolishing the Low Pay Commission (LPC), the independent body that recommends the yearly increase. It also recommends returning employer national insurance contributions to pre-April 2025 levels and reinstating the two-year qualifying period for unfair dismissal, which was abolished under Labour’s Employment Rights Act. The paper says a five-year freeze could result in an increase of about 270,000 young people in work, by suggesting that for every 1 percentage point increase in the minimum wage there is a a 0.37 percentage point decrease in the youth employment rate.
/society/2026/nov/05/milburn-review-jobs.trail: Labour says idea is ‘tin-eared’ as report says fixing rate will cost low-paid workers almost £9,000 over five years
